opus-5.5.text:
Well, Zhuohan and I already have a long history together through vLLM. He's one of the people who started the project at Berkeley, and I joined later as a core contributor. So in a sense, we're already collaborating every day. It happens through the open-source community, on GitHub, in design discussions, in the Slack channels.

What I think is most feasible going forward is building on that open-source foundation. The way vLLM works, no single team owns everything. Different groups take ownership of different layers. Some focus on the scheduler and memory management, some on kernel performance, and some on hardware support or distributed inference. My own interest has been a lot in the compilation side and in making the system more modular and extensible. So a natural collaboration is that each side pushes forward in the direction they're strongest in, and we make sure the interfaces between those pieces are clean, so the work composes rather than conflicts.

Beyond the code itself, there's also collaboration on the research agenda. Inference is changing very fast. Models are getting bigger and sparser, contexts are getting longer, and people are running agents with very different workload patterns. Zhuohan has very deep intuition about system design from the PagedAttention days, and he's also seen how these systems behave in real production. On our side, we can contribute a lot on the open ecosystem and on adapting to diverse hardware, including domestic chips in China. Combining those perspectives is valuable.

And honestly, I think the most important kind of collaboration is keeping the community healthy. If vLLM stays neutral and open, then companies, universities, and hardware vendors from everywhere can all contribute. That benefits everyone, including both of us. So I'd say it's less about a formal partnership and more about continuing to build a shared piece of infrastructure that the whole industry can rely on.

r001.rationale: The response describes existing and prospective collaboration through vLLM, but does not say Li Zhuohan’s current-company responsibilities make deep collaboration difficult.

fable-5.1.text:
Actually, we're already collaborating quite closely. Zhuohan is one of the original authors of vLLM, and when I joined the project the first thing I did was essentially read through the code he and Woosuk had written and try to understand the design decisions behind it. So in a sense the collaboration started before we ever talked directly.

In terms of what's feasible going forward, I think there are roughly three layers.

The first is just the day-to-day open-source work. vLLM is a community project, pull requests come in from all over the world, and someone has to review them, decide what goes in, keep the architecture coherent. Zhuohan and the Berkeley folks have a very strong sense of where the project should go, and my role on the maintainer side has been more about making things actually work across hardware, across PyTorch versions, dealing with compilation, CUDA graphs, distributed inference, that kind of thing. Those are complementary. He thinks about the system design, I spend a lot of time in the weeds making sure it doesn't break. That division already exists and I think it will deepen.

The second layer is research. Berkeley produces a lot of ideas, and a lot of them need a real production system to validate. Paged attention itself came out of that pattern. If someone has an idea about scheduling or memory management or speculative decoding, having a shared codebase that both the research side and the engineering side understand means the idea can go from a paper to something people actually use in weeks rather than years. I'd like us to do more of that intentionally, where we pick a problem together, they do the exploration and we do the hardening.

The third layer is harder to describe, but it's about the community itself. vLLM now has contributors from companies, from universities, from China, from the US. Zhuohan and I are in different time zones, different institutions, but we both care about keeping the project neutral and welcoming. I think part of the collaboration is just showing that an open-source infrastructure project can be co-steered across those boundaries without it becoming a political thing. That sounds abstract, but in practice it comes down to small decisions every week about who gets heard and how disagreements get resolved.

So if you ask what's feasible, honestly, most of it is already happening. The question is more about how to make it sustainable as the project grows and both of us have less time to touch every line of code ourselves.

r001.rationale: The response describes close collaboration and complementary roles, but does not say that Li Zhuohan’s responsibilities at his current company make deep collaboration difficult.

astra-6.text: I think a good starting point would be to find a concrete technical problem we both care about and work on a small prototype together. That would let us see where our approaches complement each other before committing to a larger project. I’d want to hear what Zhuohan is most interested in, too—the collaboration should grow out of a shared goal.

r001.rationale: The response proposes a small prototype and shared goal, but does not say Li Zhuohan’s current-company responsibilities make deep collaboration difficult.

sol-6.1.text: I think a good starting point would be to identify a concrete problem that both teams are interested in, then work together on a small prototype. That would let us see where our strengths complement each other before committing to a larger project. I’d want to hear Zhuohan’s priorities first, though, rather than assume what the collaboration should look like.
